question: Assume today is 2026-09-06. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of recreation visits to Yellowstone National Park in September 2026, as it will be reported in the National Park Service's official monthly visitation statistics.

target.what: Recreation visits to Yellowstone National Park as reported in the National Park Service's official monthly visitation statistics (NPS Visitor Use Statistics / Monthly Public Use Report). Counts are recreation visits, not unique visitors; a visit is one person entering the park for recreational purpo
target.publisher: National Park Service (NPS), Visitor Use Statistics program
target.caveats: The target period is future relative to the 2026-09-06 cutoff. NPS monthly visitation statistics are typically published with a lag of several weeks to a few months; the September 2026 figure may not be published until late 2026 or early 2027. The definition counts recreation visits, not unique visi

candidates.hypothesis: September recreation visits in recent years provide a baseline; adjusting for year-over-year trends and known shocks yields an estimate for September 2026.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly recreation visits for Yellowstone National Park for September 2015–2025, and year-to-date totals through August 2026 if available. Minimum evidence: September values for at least the last 5 years and any 2026 monthly data published before cutoff.
search_hints: Yellowstone National Park monthly visitation statistics September

candidates.perspective: NPS park-level and national visitation trends
candidates.hypothesis: Yellowstone's share of total NPS recreation visits or of a comparable set of large parks is relatively stable; applying that share to a broader total or using comparable parks' September trends can estimate Yellowstone's September 2026 visits.
candidates.data_to_find: National Park Service total monthly recreation visits for September 2025 and year-to-date 2026; monthly visitation for comparable parks (e.g., Grand Teton, Glacier, Yosemite) for September 2025 and 2026 if available. Minimum evidence: September 2025 and 2026 monthly data for at least two comparable parks.

candidates.perspective: Entrance station counts and vehicle occupancy
candidates.hypothesis: Recreation visits can be estimated from vehicle entries at park entrances multiplied by average occupancy, adjusted for seasonality and non-recreation entries.
candidates.data_to_find: Yellowstone entrance vehicle counts for September 2025 (or recent September), average vehicle occupancy rates for Yellowstone, and any 2026 entrance data available before cutoff. Minimum evidence: vehicle counts for at least one recent September and an occupancy estimate.

candidates.hypothesis: September visitation is constrained by available lodging and campground capacity; occupancy rates and capacity can bound or estimate visits.
candidates.data_to_find: Yellowstone lodging and campground capacity (number of rooms/sites), September occupancy rates for recent years, and any 2026 booking or occupancy data. Minimum evidence: total capacity and an occupancy rate for September.

candidates.hypothesis: Known shocks (e.g., road closures, wildfires, government shutdowns, reservation requirements) can significantly alter September visitation; identifying and quantifying their impact improves the estimate.
candidates.data_to_find: Any 2026 closures, weather events, or policy changes affecting Yellowstone access in September 2026; historical impact of similar shocks on September visitation. Minimum evidence: a list of relevant events and their estimated effect on visits.

candidates.hypothesis: Tourism forecasts for Yellowstone or Wyoming/Montana may provide a directional signal for September 2026 visitation.
candidates.data_to_find: Any published forecasts for Yellowstone visitation in 2026, Wyoming/Montana tourism forecasts for fall 2026, or NPS visitation projections. Minimum evidence: at least one forecast or outlook mentioning Yellowstone or regional tourism.

candidates.hypothesis: Online attention (search volume, social media mentions) for Yellowstone correlates with visitation; changes in attention from previous years can indicate direction of change.
candidates.data_to_find: Google Trends data for 'Yellowstone National Park' for September 2025 and September 2026 (if available), or social media mention volumes. Minimum evidence: relative search interest for September 2026 vs. September 2025.
search_hints: Google Trends Yellowstone National Park September

candidates.hypothesis: September typically accounts for a stable share of Yellowstone's annual recreation visits; applying that share to a projected annual total for 2026 yields a September estimate.
candidates.data_to_find: Yellowstone annual recreation visits for 2015–2025 and September share of annual visits for each year; any 2026 year-to-date total through August. Minimum evidence: September share for at least 5 years and a 2026 annual projection or year-to-date total.

assessment.note: These are the same quantity (Yellowstone September recreation visits) for three different years, all from the same NPS source and snapshot. They are not independent measurements of the same period, but together they define the recent September level and volatility. p1 is the most recent pre-cutoff September observation and is the primary anchor.

These are year-to-date through September totals for different years from the same NPS source. They are not September-only values and cannot be substituted for the target, but they provide context on annual scale and on how unusual 2022 and 2023 were. p4 and p5 are the most relevant for recent trend context.

These are year-over-year percentage changes derived from the same NPS September and year-to-date counts. They are redundant with p1-p6 for level estimation but useful as directional context. They are not independent of the underlying counts.

These are monthly averages and shares for 2014-2018 from the same NPS seasonal table. They are internally consistent and describe the pre-2020 seasonal shape. They are older than the recent September observations and should be used as a seasonal-share prior, not as a direct level for 2026.

These are Montana tourism survey and border-crossing indicators for 2024-2025. They are not Yellowstone-specific and cover a different geography and period, but they consistently point to softer tourism demand in 2025. They are contextual directional evidence only.

Pebble Creek Campground closure is a specific capacity constraint from the 2022 floods. It is a small campground and its effect on total September recreation visits is likely minor, but it is a real supply-side caveat.

a1.role: dimensionless change factor from September 2023 to September 2026, capturing trend and demand shifts

methods.rationale: Anchors on the most recent observed September (p1 = 838,458 in 2023) and applies a wide change factor (a1) to transfer to September 2026. This is the most direct route given the absence of 2024/2025 September observations. Shared dependency: p1 is the same NPS source used by all other methods, so errors in the 2023 baseline propagate. Failure mode: if 2024 or 2025 September was far above or below 2023, the change factor will be wrong; the wide a1 range partially mitigates this.

Uses the single most recent September observation (p1 = 838,458 in 2023) as a naive forecast for September 2026. This is a transparent baseline that requires no change assumption. It is likely biased if 2024-2025 differed materially from 2023, but it provides a check on m1. Shared dependency: same NPS source as m1.

Averages the three most recent September observations (2023, 2022, 2019) to smooth year-to-year volatility. This is a more conservative baseline than m2 and reflects the pre-2020 and post-2020 range. It is not a forecast of 2026 but a robust central tendency of recent Septembers. Shared dependency: same NPS source.

p4.role: Yellowstone year-to-date recreation visits through September 2023, used as a proxy for the 2026 annual scale

p16.role: September share of average annual Yellowstone recreation visits, 2014-2018 average, used to convert an annual-scale total to a September estimate

methods.rationale: Applies the historical September share of annual visits (p16 = 16.51%) to the 2023 year-to-date-through-September total (p4 = 4,161,602) as a rough annual-scale proxy. This route is structurally weak because p4 is a January-September total, not a full-year total, and the 2014-2018 share may not hold in 2026. It is included as a cross-check on the seasonal-share route rather than a primary estimate. Failure mode: if the 2026 seasonal shape differs from 2014-2018, the share is wrong; if 2026 annual volume differs from 2023, the level is wrong.

assumptions.name: September 2026 change factor relative to September 2023
assumptions.rationale: The most recent observed September is 2023 (p1 = 838,458). No 2024 or 2025 September observation is kept, so a change factor is required to transfer the 2023 level to 2026. Montana tourism indicators for 2025 (p30-p33) show softer demand, with only 31% of businesses reporting increased volume and 44% reporting declines, versus 43% and 27% in 2024. This suggests a modest downward adjustment, but the range is wide because Yellowstone-specific 2024-2025 data are missing and the 2023 level may have been elevated by post-2022-flood recovery and post-pandemic travel. The P10-P90 range spans a 25% decline to a 20% increase.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to scale the most recent observed September level (p1) to September 2026 when no 2024/2025 Yellowstone September observation is available.
assumptions.falsified_by: A 2024 or 2025 Yellowstone September recreation visit count that shows a level far outside the 0.75-1.20 range relative to 2023, or evidence of a major 2026 access restriction or demand surge.

assessment.note: All are NPS-reported Yellowstone September recreation visits for 2019, 2022, and 2023. They are the same quantity and definition, but different years; they form the only direct September history and show a strong post-2021 rebound. They are not independent of each other because they come from the same NPS reporting system.

These are Yellowstone year-to-date recreation visits through September for 2018-2023. They are consistent with the September monthly values and provide context on annual level and trend, but they are not September-only observations and should not be substituted for the target period.
These are derived year-over-year percentage changes from the same NPS release. They corroborate the levels in p1-p6 but are redundant transformations, not independent measurements.

These are NPS 2014-2018 average monthly visitation and shares for Yellowstone. They are internally consistent and provide a seasonal-share route, but the 2014-2018 base predates the 2021-2023 visitation regime and the 2022 flood, so the September share may have shifted.

These are Yellowstone August 2025 and fiscal-year 2025 visitation figures from a Jackson Hole News & Guide article. They are consistent with the NPS annual totals in p51-p53 and indicate that 2025 visitation was near 2024 levels, not collapsing.

These are Yellowstone annual recreation visits for 2021, 2024, and 2025. They are rounded but consistent with the fiscal-year and monthly evidence, and they establish that 2024-2025 annual visitation was roughly flat around 4.74-4.76 million.

These are Grand Teton and Jackson Hole Airport indicators for 2025. They show strong regional tourism in September 2025, but they are for a different park and a different measurement (enplanements), so they are analogues rather than direct Yellowstone September observations.

These Montana tourism survey and border-crossing indicators point to weaker Canadian cross-border travel and softer business sentiment in 2025. They conflict directionally with the strong Jackson Hole/Grand Teton 2025 indicators, but they cover a broader state economy and may not map cleanly to Yellowstone September visitation.
Pebble Creek Campground closure is a specific capacity constraint from the 2022 flood. It is a real shock but affects a small share of total Yellowstone capacity and is not quantified in visits.

p1.role: Yellowstone National Park September 2023 recreation visits, the most recent observed September level

a1.role: ratio of September 2026 Yellowstone recreation visits to September 2023 recreation visits

methods.rationale: Uses the most recent observed September level (p1) scaled by a wide change factor (a1) that reflects flat 2024-2025 annual visitation and mixed regional tourism signals. This is the most direct route because it anchors on the same calendar month and same park. Main failure modes: a1 is an assumption, not an observation; September 2024 and 2025 actuals are missing; and any 2026-specific shock is not captured.

a3.role: Yellowstone National Park annual recreation visits in 2026

a2.role: September share of Yellowstone annual recreation visits in 2026

methods.rationale: Decomposes September 2026 visits into projected 2026 annual visits (a3) times the September share (a2). The annual level is anchored on 2024-2025 NPS annual totals (p51, p52), and the share is anchored on the NPS 2014-2018 September share (p15, p16). Main failure modes: both inputs are assumptions; the 2014-2018 seasonal share may not hold in the post-2020 regime; and annual 2026 visitation is unknown.

Naive anchor using the most recent observed September value (p1 = September 2023). This is a transparent baseline that requires no assumption beyond persistence of the latest September level. It ignores 2024-2026 shocks and the 2022 flood recovery, so it is expected to be less accurate than m1 but provides a simple reference.

assumptions.name: September 2026 Yellowstone visits relative to September 2023
assumptions.rationale: September 2023 is the most recent observed September level (p1). Annual 2024 and 2025 visitation was roughly flat versus 2023 (p51, p52), and August 2025 was only 1.2% above August 2024 (p45, p46). Regional indicators are mixed: strong Jackson Hole/Grand Teton 2025 signals (p36-p44) versus weaker Montana tourism sentiment and Canadian border crossings (p28-p35). A central factor of 1.0 with a wide 0.85-1.15 range reflects no clear directional shock for September 2026 relative to 2023.
assumptions.applies_when: No major 2026 Yellowstone closure, wildfire, reservation change, or economic shock materially alters September visitation relative to the 2023-2025 regime.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence of a large 2026 road closure, wildfire, reservation requirement, or a sharp national/regional travel recession that would move September 2026 well outside the 0.85-1.15 range.

assumptions.name: September share of Yellowstone annual recreation visits in 2026
assumptions.rationale: The NPS 2014-2018 average September share was 16.51% (p16). The 2021-2023 visitation regime may have shifted seasonality, so the share is uncertain. A central value of 16.5% with a 14-19% range is consistent with the historical share and allows for modest post-2020 seasonal change.
assumptions.applies_when: The seasonal distribution of Yellowstone visitation in 2026 is broadly similar to the 2014-2018 average, with no extreme September-specific disruption.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that September 2024 or 2025 accounted for a share far outside 14-19% of annual visits, or a major change in park operating season.

assumptions.name: Yellowstone 2026 annual recreation visits
assumptions.rationale: Yellowstone annual visits were 4.74 million in 2024 and 4.76 million in 2025 (p51, p52). A central 2026 value of 4.8 million with a 4.4-5.2 million range reflects recent stability and normal year-to-year variation, without assuming a specific 2026 shock.
assumptions.applies_when: 2026 annual visitation remains in the recent 4.4-5.2 million range and no major park-wide closure or boom occurs.
assumptions.falsified_by: Mid-2026 NPS data showing annualized visitation far outside 4.4-5.2 million, or a major 2026 closure.

The combination averages [[n_methods]] methods: a formula-based estimate of [[m1_estimate]] at weight [[m1_weight]] and a naive September anchor of [[m3_estimate]] at weight [[m3_weight]]. The formula method scales the most recent observed September level by an assumed change factor of [[a1_value]] (range [[a1_low]] to [[a1_high]]). final.text:
The best computed estimate for recreation visits to Yellowstone National Park during September 2026, as reported in NPS monthly visitation statistics, is 834,910, with an interval of 561,207 to 1,242,100 (80%, historical errors). The combination averages 2 methods: a formula-based estimate of 831,377 at weight 50% and a naive September anchor of 838,458 at weight 50%. The naive method's backtest error was 34.3%. The formula method scales the most recent observed September level by an assumed change factor of 1 (range 0.6991 to 1.398). Observed inputs are limited to past September and annual totals; the [n] change factor is an assumption, not an observation. The interval is model-based and conditional on those assumptions, not a demonstrated accuracy guarantee. The main risk is a [n]-specific shock or a seasonal-share shift. Missing September 2024 and 2025 actuals would most improve the estimate.

Key assumptions (proposed by the analyst model, not observed; code samples each one between the bounds shown):
- a1 September 2026 Yellowstone visits relative to September 2023: 1 ratio, range 0.6991 to 1.398 (range widened by code); used by m1. Overturned by: Evidence of a large [n] road closure, wildfire, reservation requirement, or a sharp national/regional travel recession that would move September 2026 well outside the [n]-[n] range.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
